name: Utility Tree Construction
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Pruning the Forest: How ATAM Builds and Prioritizes a Utility Tree
lesson.summary: Utility tree construction organizes dozens of quality attribute scenarios into a prioritized hierarchy, so an ATAM review spends its limited time on the handful of scenarios that matter most to the business and are hardest to achieve.
lesson.body:
A utility tree is a hierarchy with utility at the root, quality attributes such as performance, security, availability, and modifiability as the first branch level, refinements of each attribute as the next level, and individual quality attribute scenarios as the leaves. Utility tree construction is the activity of building that hierarchy from the raw scenarios a stakeholder workshop produced, then labeling every leaf with two ratings, typically high, medium, or low: how important the scenario is to the business, and how difficult it is expected to be for the architecture to satisfy.

The two ratings are what make the tree useful rather than just organized. A scenario rated high importance and high difficulty, for instance a proof of stake blockchain surviving a coordinated exit of one third of staked validators without halting block production, is exactly where an ATAM team should spend its limited analysis time, because it is both consequential and architecturally uncertain. A scenario rated low importance and low difficulty, say the block explorer UI rendering correctly on an older mobile browser, can be acknowledged and set aside without further discussion. The tree turns a flat list of eighty scenarios into a small number of high, high leaves worth deep analysis.

Building the tree for a blockchain system typically starts with the four or five quality attributes stakeholders raised most often during scenario generation. Under security, refinements might include consensus integrity and key management. Under availability, refinements might include node connectivity resilience and network partition tolerance. Under performance, refinements might include transaction throughput and confirmation latency. Under modifiability, refinements might include the cost of shipping a hard fork, tying this concept directly back to how disruptive a protocol upgrade turns out to be in practice.

A worked branch makes this concrete. Under performance, then throughput, the leaf scenario reads: during a viral NFT mint, ten thousand simultaneous transaction submissions must still see ninety five percent confirm within twenty minutes at a predictable fee. Stakeholders might rate this high importance, since it directly affects user trust and adoption, and high difficulty, since fee markets under contention are a known hard problem. That high, high rating earns the scenario a place in the small set the ATAM team analyzes in depth, tracing it through the actual architecture to look for the sensitivity points and tradeoff points covered next.

The discipline of rating every leaf, rather than letting the loudest stakeholder's favorite scenario dominate, is what keeps utility tree construction honest. A blockchain team can be tempted to rate their weakest area as low importance simply because they have no good answer for it; a facilitator's job during construction is to push back when a rating looks driven by discomfort rather than genuine business priority.
